INTERNATIONAL convention limiting manufacture AND REGULATING DISTRIBUTION

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That it is expedient that parliament do approve of the international convention for limiting the manufacture and regulating the distribution of narcotic drugs, Geneva, July 13, 1931, signed on behalf of Canada by the plenipotentiaries named therein, and that this house do approve of the same.
He said: In moving the resolution which stands in my name, I desire to make a short

explanation inasmuch as this convention is a matter of considerable importance to the dominion. It was drawn up by an international conference held in Geneva, from the 27th May to the 13th July, 1931, in which fifty-seven states participated. Thirty-eight have now signed the convention.
The convention was signed for Canada by Dr. W. A. Riddell, Canadian advisory officer accredited to the League of Nations, and Colonel C. H. L. Sharman, chief of the narcotic division of the Department of Pensions and National Health, who represented this country at the conference.
The convention will become effective ninety days after the secretary-general of the League of Nations has received the ratifi-caton or accessions of twenty-five members of the League of Nations or non-member States, including any four of the following: France, Germany, United Kingdom, Japan, the Netherlands, Switzerland, Turkey, and the United States of America, which, of course, is not a member of the League.
Seven of the eight named states, that is all except Turkey, (have already signed the convention, and His Majesty's government in the United Kingdom has introduced legislation which is now before the British parliament to give effect to the provisions of the convention.
The convention supplements and develops the earlier efforts for the international regulation of the traffic in narcotic drugs which were embodied in the Hague Convention of the 23rd January, 1912, and the Geneva Convention of the 19th February, 1923, to both of which the Dominion of Canada is a party. Under the provisions of the conventions now in force a fairly effective system of control of international trade in narcotic drugs has been worked out, and I suppose, Mr. Speaker, that there are few matters of more universal import to this country than the trade in narcotic drugs. The main lines of this system of control are probably familiar to the members of this house, for on more than one occasion we have debated the matter. They are embodied in the Opium and Narcotic Drug Act and the regulations made by order in council to give effect to that act. In substance, they require that all imports of narcotic drugs into this country should be accompanied by an official import 'certificate issued by a competent government department, which has satisfied itself that the consignment in question will be used solely for medicinal purposes. Within the limits of the earlier agreements this system has worked satisfactorily, but it was obvious that no system of control of 'trade could be

Narcotic Drugs
completely effective if no restrictions of any kind were placed upon the manufacture of drugs whose distribution was regulated. It will be recalled that on more than one occasion the medical doctors who are members of this chamber have discussed that phase of the situation, and the difficulty of adequate control based upon restrictions was apparent when no control or restrictions were exercised upon manufacture. That discussion, I think, will be within the memory of most members of the chamber.
The task of inducing the manufacturing countries to agree upon restricting their output of habit-forming drugs has been an extremely difficult one. The kernel of the convention before the house is Article 6, which stipulates:
1. There shall not be manufactured in any country or territory in any one year a quantity of any of the drugs greater than the total of the following quantities:	.	.
(a)	The quantity required within the limits
of the estimates for that country or territory for that year for use as such for its medicinal and scientific needs including the quantity required for the manufacture of preparations for the export of which export authorizations are not required, whether such preparations are intended for domestic consumption or for export.	....
(b)	The quantity required within the limits of the estimates for that country or territory for that year for conversion, whether for domestic consumption or for export.
(c)	Such quantity as may be required by that country or territory for the execution during the year of orders for export in accordance with the provisions of this convention.
(d) The quantity, if any, required by that country or territory for the purpose of maintaining the reserve stocks at the level specified for the estimates for that year.
(e)	The quantity, if any, required for the purpose of maintaining the government stocks at the level specified in the estimates for that year.
An extensive illicit traffic in such drugs as morphine, heroin, and cocaine is carried on in many parts of the world. In fact, almost every day one reads in the newspapers of efforts that are being made to convict those who are so engaged. We in this country are neither exempt from the operation of these habit-forming drugs nor yet from the illicit traffic in them, but our efforts to repress the traffic have been marked with a certain measure of success. The effectiveness of regulatory action has, however, been limited by the fact that narcotic drugs are being manufactured in quantities vastly in excess of legitimate requirements for medical and scientific purposes. The restriction of manufacture to these requirements is the primary object of the convention before the house. Its
prompt ratification and rigorous application promise the ultimate eradication of a wretched and evil trade.
The importance of securing a satisfactory solution of this problem of manufacture to a country like Canada, which is technically a "victim country" cannot be over-emphasized. We do not manufacture narcotic drugs but depend for our legitimate requirements upon the countries in which these industries are already established. It is, therefore, a source of great satisfaction to all engaged in preventive work in Canada that an agreement has been reached on such a measure of limitation as this convention represents.
I may say that our representatives at the convention at Geneva were confronted with many difficulties in securing assistance from countries similarly situated and lending assistance to other countries determined to suppress the traffic. The result is the convention now before the house. It will be necessary to amend the Opium and Narcotic Drug Aot of 1929, and notice to that effect stands upon the order paper. That will enable the ratification of the convention, which will take place immediately, and the bill, as I say, will give effect to the provisions which the convention provides.
It may be pointed out that if this convention is approved and the government authorized to proceed to its ratification Canada will be the first country to complete ratification of the convention.
The attached report may be of some interest to members of this house who have been following these matters, for these words were used at the fifth committee of the assembly of the League of Nations on September 18, 1931, and give a fair indication of public opinion as represented by the delegates there assembled. The language is as follows:
The convention marks an entirely new and highly important development in international cooperation, since this is the first time that an industry has been brought under international regulation and that manufacture in its economic aspect has been wholly subordinated to higher humanitarian and moral aims. Thanks to the system established by this convention and the Geneva convention, there will be at the headquarters of the league itself a sort of central counting-house for the world traffic in drugs. . . . The new convention covers a far larger number of drugs than preceding conventions. It brings codeine under control, whereas for many years morphine converted into codeine has to some extent escaped all supervision. It prohibits the export, except on very strict conditions, of a substance which has in the past bulked very large in the illicit traffic-diacetylmorphme- and raises the question of its replacement by

League of Nations

less dangerous substances. It contains stipulations relating to reserve stocks and surplus stocks, which will be gradually brought into use for legitimate consumption by a corresponding reduction in output or will be disposed of under the sole responsibility of the government.
Above all, through a system of estimates furnished by governments, the convention enables a world total of the quantities to be manufactured to be fixed, and sets up a supervisory body to examine those estimates. . . . The new convention strengthens the powers of various league organizations, especially the advisory committee and the permanent central board. The fifth committee emphasized the importance that attached to the provisions instructing the advisory committee to draw up a model administrative code to serve, as it were, as a body of regulations for the application of the convention, and as a pattern for national laws and regulations. Furthermore, the system of annual reports and reports of seizures, which forms an essential part of the committee's work, is for the first time effectually incorporated in an international convention. The powers and responsibilities of the permanent central board are also enlarged.
Those are the words used in submitting the convention to the assembly in September last. I have, therefore, Mr. Speaker, the greatest satisfaction in moving the approval of this convention which has been entered into and in connection with which I should like to say that the Canadian representatives, and especially the chief of the narcotic division of our own Department of Pensions and National Health took a very important and at times not indecisive part.

Motion agreed to.

Resolved, that it is expedient to introduce a measure to authorize deductions of ten per cent from the amounts of certain salaries or other compensations or indemnities payable by the government of Canada during the fiscal year 1932-33.
And to provide for payment out of the consolidated revenue fund of all current contributions payable under the provisions of the Civil Service Superannuation Act in respect of the salaries payable during the fiscal year ending March 31, 1933, of all employees who receive not more than one thousand two hundred dollars per annum.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, when the house adjourned last night at eleven o'clock I had stated I felt it was inevitable that this resolution should be accepted by the house. I did urge the government however to reduce interest charges on money or, as it is commonly known, money wages. I do not think there is any justice in reducing the salaries and wages of 90 per cent of the people of Canada and at the same time increasing money wages. We are moving in opposite directions.
I then proceeded to protest against some of the exemptions proposed in the resolution. I can see no reason why lieutenant governors' salaries should not be reduced, or why judges' salaries should not be reduced. They are the very highest paid officials and in such times as these their salaries could very well be reduced. I wish however particularly to refer to the military officers whose salaries under the proposed resolution are exempt. I can see no reason for such exemptions. It would seem that military men are being exempted while the salaries of civil employees are being cut; thousands of civil servants are to receive cuts in their salaries. Some of those servants were in the forces overseas; some of them served four years in the great war, and made great sacrifices. For that service they received the handsome salary of SI .10 a day, after which they returned to Canada and were placed in the civil service. Now they ai'e to receive a ten per cent cut, while the military officers, the generals and colonels who drew high salaries during the war are to be

allowed to maintain their regular salaries. I can think of no reason for such discrimination. Particularly do I feel that there is an injustice when I consider what is happening in the air force. Recently we learned that some of the men in that force who have been laid off sought service under a foreign government. I think they cannot be blamed for adopting that course. In most cases they have wives and children dependent upon them for support. Some of the very finest men I have known in Canada have been members of that force, and it is not necessary to remind this house that in every branch of military service Canada's soldiers were second to none among those who took part in the great war. I do not wish to make any comparison between the different branches of the Canadian military forces, but certainly I can say that Canada's air men were second to none. I believe every member of this house must admit that.
Recently a statement was made in the house that 70 officers of the Royal Canadian Air Force had been laid off. I believe 42 of them are ex-service men, and nearly 40 are married. To my mind, Mr. Speaker, this is a discrimination against married men who are also war veterans, when by common consent of all parties in this house war veterans, and especially married men, should at all times receive the greatest consideration. Forty-two returned men and dependents would number about 100 souls. I feel, Mr. Speaker, that I cannot let this resolution pass without protesting against the proposed cut. If these men are to be let out of the air force Canada is going to lose the services of her most experienced flyers. These men have flown over northwestern Canada and have charted air routes across that great country. They charted the air routes over Labrador, they laid out the routes for our air mail service. If they are to be dismissed now Canada is going to lose the very cream of her flying men. As a matter of general policy I think the government is making a mistake in reducing the civil service at this time. I realize that perhaps a cut should be made in the amount that is being spent on the civil service, but with hundreds of thousands of people unemployed surely it is not good policy to add to their ranks by discharging men of this type. I think a much better way of dealing with the matter would be to keep these men on the pay list at reduced salaries, that is, by cutting down the number of days' work so that nobody need be laid off. This would involve no increase in the appropriation for

the civil service, and all these men could be taken care of as vacancies occurred in any of the departments. We are only adding to the number of unemployed when we discharge civil servants at a time like this. I think most of us realize that there are no other jobs available for these people, which means that within a short time some of them will be in need of direct relief.

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext: Why should the taxpayer be burdened?

subtopic: PROPOSED DEDUCTION OF TEN PER CENT IN INDEMNITIES AND SALARIES
speechtext:
What I am proposing will
not add to the burden of the taxpayer. Under my proposal the reduced hours of labour would enable these men to be continued in the service without additional cost. I urge that this method be adopted to take care of these men now forming part of Canada's air force. Why should these men feel compelled to seek service under some foreign government-to provide as a matter of fact a fighting air force for that government in order to provide for their families? Flying is the only work these men are fitted for, and there are no positions in civil aviation to which they can turn now. They served in the war when they were young, in the very best years of their life, the formative period as we term it, and they are not fitted for any other work. For the work of our air force, however, they are better qualified than any other men whom we could put in their place.
Again I urge the government to adopt my suggestion that these men be retained in the service at a reduced salary. I am sure they would not object to a reduction in salary. Naturally they feel that they are not being treated fairly. A reduction of ten per cent applied to the salaries of all the officers of the National Defence department would take care of the salaries of these forty married men, all of them ex-servicemen, under the proposal which I am now putting forward. If the government will not consider such a reduction in the salaries of the personnel of the National Defence department, I suggest that these men be retained, and the total amount which is provided for the air force after the proposed ten per cent cut is put into operation be distributed among all the men who belong to the air force; let them all share in the reduction.
I suggest that the government abolish the lieutenant-governorships. The saving thus effected would more than take care of these forty married men and their dependents, and I am sure the service rendered Canada by

Public Service-Salary Deduction
these flying men is far more important than any service rendered to the country by our lieutenant-governors. Any judge of the supreme court in each of the provinces could very well discharge the duties of lieutenant-governor. Surely there is no question as to which is the more necessary national service.
I might also point out that a reduction of ten per cent in judges' salaries would provide far more than is being saved by the discharge of these flying men.
May I say in conclusion that these men have done the most dangerous work of any branch of the civil service. But what is the reward they are receiving? They are not being asked to submit to a cut of ten per cent; they are being retired, in most cases at one month's notice. If they return to civil life it is impossible for them to get jobs as flying men, the activities of civil aviation being now at a minimum. In a word, these men are facing unemployment-a most distressing prospect for their wives and families. These flying men have given Canada their best. Is Canada now going to let them be turned out in the cold? I do hope the government will take some action to see that these men are retained in the service.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before this debate closes,
I wish to add a few comments with reference to this resolution which does not do honour to the government. It is useless to refer to the numerous pledges made throughout the country by the Conservative party in the last election; pledges of charlatans, made with the view of capturing the people's confidence, pledges according to which the serious problem of unemployment was to be solved in three days, and an opportunity would be afforded to farmers to sell their products at better prices and secure new markets for our manufactures. It will soon be two years since this government has taken over the affairs of the country. The economic depression which existed at the last election far from abating has become worse. This is a clear proof of this government's incompetence and shows up their lack of ability to govern the country.
In order to balance its budget, it asks this house through a resolution to cut the salaries of civil servants by ten per cent.
The principle upon which rests this resolution, that is a horizontal cut applied to all salaries is no surprise to me. Ever since this government has been in power it has always been the poor, the small wage earner and the humble citizens who were called upon to contribute and in the same measure as the wealthy, the millionaires that sit in large numbers on your right, sir. They are responsible for the present state of our finances through the enforcement of a high protective tariff.
The quota of the civil servants who receive $1,200 per year, in justice should be less than that of the official who is paid $5,000 or $10,000. In fact, those receiving $1,200 should be entirely exempt from contributing to the treasury. As to judges, it would only be fair, during this depression that they do their bit in helping the state, they should not be exempt. The same may be said as regards gold lace officers who travel around the country and who perhaps have not even won their spurs on the battlefield. And these millionaires who sit facing us and have never known the sweat of labour, should also contribute on a larger scale than the wage-earners in order to relieve the present economic depression. It does not behoove the latter to open their purse, but those who have large fortunes and surpluses they cannot spend should contribute largely.
For these reasons, sir, I am opposed to this resolution, and not because I am called upon to contribute $400, as my share-I can well afford making this sacrifice-however, I strongly protest against this resolution which forces the small wage earner to contribute in the same ratio as those who can better afford it.
Yesterday, I heard the hon. member for St. Henri (Mr. Mercier) state: "Those who should be taxed for the administration of the country are those who have inherited millions through estates." I shall add that is also those who during the war-and they are friends of the present government-built up fortunes by selling horses, bacon, drugs and scrap iron, and, to-day, travel over the country displaying the millions they accumulated at the expense of the poor soldier who on the battlefield shed his blood to uphold freedom. Let the millionaires who accumulated their wealth during the war open widely their purse, and let us not allow the government to put through a resolution which asks the small wage earners, the lower grade civil servants to contribute equally with those who are in receipt of $10,000 or over $15,000 per year. In this contribution, one must not forget those who, last year, voted themselves $2,000 in prevision of this ten per cent cut which they are called upon to contribute in order to help the country out of the hole where this government has placed it, an administration directly opposed to the true interests of the Canadian people.

This is why, sir, I am strongly opposed to this resolution. If the situation is so bad that civil servants' salaries must be reduced, let it be at least in proportion to their earnings. I trust that these few remarks will be received in the best of spirit by the government and they will realize that if they wish to truly serve the people, and have at heart to do justice to all, they will, when the bill comes before the house, have it drawn up in such a way as to deal fairly with the small wage earners and that the latter will only be called upon to contribute in proportion to their earnings. In closing my remarks I would ask the government to exempt not only those who earn SI,200 but to also include those earning $1,500 and even $1,800. Should they grant my request I shall support the resolution. Otherwise, should they persist in being unfair to the small wage earners, I shall oppose it, and publicly I shall say: Stop 1 Do not ask from the humble and small wage earner the same contribution as you ask from those who are high up, rich and millionaires. The former are entitled to be fairly treated and as legislators we should see that they are.

I am quite

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
With respect to the last
question submitted by my right hon. friend, of course there was discussion with any number of civil servants. My right hon. friend will realize that while there is a civil service federation, a highly reputable and very representative body, it by no means represents the whole body of the civil service of Canada. We heard, as a government, a deputation from the civil service federation, as well as any others who cared to make representations to us, so I think it is a fair statement, without the government being called upon to consult every individual civil servant in Canada, to say that there was a reasonable and fair canvass made of the situation prior to this resolution being brought in.
Now I must take exception, quite deferentially, to my right hon. friend calling in question the procedure of the government in bringing down a bill of this character and assuming that parliament must pass it. My right hon. friend knows full well that it is the responsibility of the ministry of the day to initiate legislation touching financial matters, and we followed the procedure which my right hon. friend has followed and which of necessity all governments must follow. The answer to the objection he raised will be found in the circumstances as to whether or not parliament in its wisdom sees fit to pass legislation which has been initiated by the government. If it does so then his question will be answered, and in that case I can see no force in the suggestion he makes.

May I say
that in speaking of the civil service being given an opportunity voluntarily to make a contribution to meet the emergent situation, similar to the way in which members of parliament are doing at the moment, I had in mind what I observed during last year and this year, that members of the public service had made a very considerable voluntary contribution to unemployment relief. I understand that a collection was taken up in the different departments and that members of the service contributed very generously towards unemployment relief. In doing so I think the public service showed that if given the same opportunity it was just as ready to make its contribution to meet an emergent situation as are members of parliament.
In that same connection I should like to ask another question. Did the ministry, before it brought in this measure, confer with the Civil Service Commission as to whether or not, in their opinion, a horizontal cut would be a wise way of bringing about this deduction, or whether in the interests of the public service of Canada it would be better to have a graded deduction?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
My right hon. friend has
referred to the civil servants having made contributions towards the unemployment relief fund. They did so, and they are to be commended for their action in that respect. I have always found that civil servants, wherever they may be, are splendid citizens, and as citizens and not as civil servants they made a contribution to that philanthropic object, together with other citizens. But my right hon. friend must bear in mind that the contribution was made from the salary which they had received in full. If this bill passes, the contribution for which we are asking will

be made out of the amount of the salary which they will receive for the next year, and therefore it has no bearing upon the suggestion he has just made with respect to their already having made a contribution, unless he takes the ground that having made a contribution this year they are to be absolved for all time from making any further contribution.
Then with respect to the other question, so far as I am aware the Civil Service Commission was not consulted as to whether it would be wiser to make a straight reduction of ten per cent or whether it would be better to have that reduction graduated. The commission may have been consulted, but so far as I am aware it was not. However, my right hon. friend knows that whether the proposed method is the right one or the wrong one, after all it is a question of governmental policy, for which the government must assume the responsibility. It may be that my right hon. leader consulted the Civil Service Commission upon that point; I cannot say.

As I have said very frequently, if there is a wrong way of going about anything the Prime Minister is apt to take it in preference to the right way. I repeat that the Prime Minister's method is very arbitrary. It is not the method, before taking a particular step, of bringing into consultation and conference those who may be affected. What the Minister of Finance now says bears out the truth of that statement. Apparently the minister personally has not been consulted, nor does he know whether or not that step has 'been taken with the Civil Service Commission; I venture to say there is not a member of the .cabinet at this moment who can say whether or not the Civil Service Commission was consulted. The steps that lead up to the formation of government policy is something with which every member of the cabinet ought to be familiar; what has been done ought to be a matter of common knowledge on the part- of the ministry,-the ministrj'' should have full knowledge,-before a step of this kind is taken which affects the entire public service of Canada. Every member of the government should know whether the body appointed by this parliament particularly for the purpose of having supervision over the public service in matters of salary deductions, salary increases and so on, had been consulted.
That is one of the very serious objections to the measure as framed, that apparently there has been no consultation with the service itself. The minister has just said that the government received a statement from the

civil service federation. I think it was admitted, on a day when my bon. friend unfortunately was prevented from being in the house, that when the delegation came to present their views this resolution was already on the order paper, and the bill itself, I understand, drafted. I do not think they were given any real opportunity to present any views in a way which 'would .permit of their careful consideration, and I do say that if that opportunity had been given I believe the ministry would not have brought in a horizontal cut. It is the horizontal cut to which we take exception. We do not take exception to the .public service being asked to make a contribution at this time, but we are opposed to a horizontal, arbitrary cut of ten per cent instead of a graded deduction. That is the whole point of our opposition to this measure; the vote just taken was registered on that account, as I made very plain when I spoke at the outset.
I do think that if the ministry had approached this matter by conference, by conciliation and by negotiation, the main object namely, that of getting a very substantial contribution from the public service of Canada, might have been attained, but it would have been obtained with good will, and with an appreciation of the fact that all those contributing were joining in the performance of a patriotic act. The civil service of Canada is just as patriotic as any other body, as my hon. friend has just said, and civil servants are just as much entitled to an opportunity to disclose their patriotism to the country as is the Prime Minister. They were quite as much entitled to be given an opportunity voluntarily to show what they were willing to do as the Prime Minister was entitled to say what should be done, whether they wished it or did not wish it done. That is the point I desire to impress on my hon. friend.
Now I should like to ask another question. There has been a civil service council established by order in council. I do not know whether or not hon. gentlemen opposite have seen the order in council, or whether they are aware of it. I think I may take it for granted that this body was not called into conference either. If I am mistaken in that, perhaps my hon. friend will correct me. That body was formed for the very purpose of helping to meet situations of this kind. It was brought into being by the previous administration, as being in character similar to the joint councils which for some time past have been in existence in England, and which have had to do with these very questions that arise between a ministry and those who are members of the public ser-

vice. I submit that this body should have been brought into conference with the government and given an opportunity to make representations. I believe that, if such a body had been consulted and the whole situation carefully .placed before it, the .ministry would have been able to come to parliament and advise us that the public service of Canada and the government had arrived at a graded basis of deduction from the salaries of civil servants, which the civil servants themselves were prepared voluntarily to make, and which the country would be pleased to know they were ready to make. The arbitrary method is what I wish to stress, the way in which the government has gone about' this business, however laudable the object may be. That is one point.
The second point is this. My hon. friend mentioned a list of those who are exempt, and at the head of the list he placed His Excellency the Governor General. speechtext:
I must respectfully take
*exception to my right hon. friend's position. He assumes that the action with respect to this measure was the arbitrary and highhanded action of the Prime Minister. We must share equally in the responsibilty. My right hon. friend would have it appear-and perhaps from his point of view I cannot take exception to his having done so-that the action of the government is arbitrary and high-handed, a take it or leave it attitude. Well, I submit that such a view could be taken of every government proposal that is brought down following constitutional practice. As I have already said this afternoon, money bills must of necessity be initiated by the government and upon message; there is no other way whereby they can be initiated. Therefore the same argument would obtain with respect to every similar measure which has been introduced not only this session but in previous sessions, and that will be the case until some other method of procedure is devised which in the judgment of British parliaments is more satisfactory than the one that obtains at the moment. My right hon. friend has put a query to me as to whether others have followed the example of His Excellency the Governor General. So far as I am aware none have.

There is just
one further point I wish to refer to and that is the conception of contractual obligation which my hon. friend has put forward-that there are certain statutes governing the salaries of some officials in the public service, and that these statutes being in existence places those to whom they refer in a different position from the others. May I ask my hon. friend:	Is it not true that every man or
woman who enters the public service does so because of certain advantages which the service offers to them, of permanency, the possibility of promotion, statutory increases, retirement and the like, in consequence of which they are prepared to accept a much lower rate of remuneration than very many of them would receive if they were in the competitive world, and taking their part in the general business of the country? bution from the civil service and you are not asking it from the other citizens of the country, I say to him: The other citizens are sustaining a cut of ten per cent and perhaps a little more.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: No.

They will have to meet the same obligations in respect of taxation as anyone else. If the government would say: We shall have a one per cent 'levy on the salary of every citizen of Canada, they would not have to make a ten per cent levy on this particular branch of the public service. That is where the discrimination comes in. As I see it, it is a most unfair and unjust discrimination, and I think the minister, when he considers the great body of citizens at large, will see the matter in the same light. There is a discrimination between members of the civil service, who have limited salaries, and lieutenant-governors, judges, members of the army and the navy, the air force and the mounted police. How can my hon. friend defend a discrimination of that kind? He began by defending it upon statutory grounds. But that is not what he is arguing now. His last argument is that, if the civil servants do not pay this, all the other citizens will have to pay it. Why should the civil service have to make a contribution on behalf of the other citizens? It is singling out one particular class in the dominion and making it carry a burden which ought to be distributed generally over the citizens at large.

I do not like to enter into the discussion of what seems to be a legal problem, but some hon. members have been considering the question of the judges. It has been indicated from the other side of the house that they are to be exempted on statutory grounds. The question of statutory grounds was raised on this side only because it was first raised on that side. Some of us who are not lawyers feel that if the argument in regard to statutory grounds holds good as to judges, it holds equally good as to civil servants.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I do not think this makes very much difference, but in my first answer to an inquiry that was submitted as to why there was a distinction, I said it was because of contractual rights; I did not mention statute. I said it was a matter of contract.
I hold in my hand a copy of the Civil Service Act, from which I wish to correct a statement made by the Minister of Justice that judges could not resign, could not get out of the service at will.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: I made no such statement.
Yes, the hon. member did. He said that their resignation need not be accepted.

Then why did the hon.
member not say that?
I was not given time to say it.
My hon. friend tells part of the truth all the time.
My hon. friend thinks he is at present in the good roads convention. He has wheels in his head.
I have as many as the hon. gentleman himself.

While the judges have the privilege of resigning, the civil service does not have it. No member of the civil service may resign except under regulations of the Civil Service Commission. That is statutory. Section 53 of the act reads:
The commission shall by regulation prescribe what shall constitute a resignation of a position by an employee.
Therefore they are in a worse position than the judges. Let me point out further that section 13 of the Civil Service Act states, in part:
But no appointment shall in any case be made at less than the minimum nor at more than the maximum rate prescribed for a class.
Is that not a statute and binding? Is that not a contract? Let me go further. Subsection 4 of section 11 states:
No permanent employee who was appointed before the tenth day of November, 1919, shall have the salary of his position on that date reduced by reason of the classification of his position, and if any such employee is placed in any class where the maximum salary is smaller than the maximum salary of the subdivision or grade in which he was before classified he shall be entitled in the same manner and to the same extent as heretofore to increases until he has reached the maximum fixed for the subdivision or grade in which he was previously classified.
That is even more binding than any contract for the judges of the supreme court or the lieutenant-governors of the provinces. The statute distinctly states that there shall be a minimum and a maximum. That minimum and that maximum are rated when the employee is engaged; he is under contract; the

I am willing if it is necessary, in the interests of -this country, but I say I am absolutely opposed to -the cut, whether it is on my indemnity or on yours, Mr. Chairman, or that of any other member of parliament. I believe it will be reflected all over this country and that when we next meet here a-fter voting to -reduce the salaries of the service by ten per cent, the country will not be one iota the better off; on the -other hand, in my opinion as a business man, -the cut will make conditions worse than they are -to-day. But I do say that if we are going to reduce anybody's salary by ten per cent, -then every man w-h-o gets a salary from this federal government, whether he be a lieutenant-governor, a judge, a commodore, a general or anybody else, should take the same reduction, and the legislation should be amended -to make the cut general throughout the whole service.

A distinction should be
made between those who are able to pay and those who are not, and then perhaps we might easily come to an agreement with the government. I entirely agree with the Minister of Finance that in this democratic country, according to law and custom, money measures are always brought into the house by the government, but this resolution has been presented to the committee to-day to give members on both sides of the house the opportunity to submit their suggestions to the government, and as has been said before, the government can either accept or reject those suggestions.
I have a suggestion to make to the government. Why not begin the cut, if it is necessary, at the figure of $4,000, and leave aside those civil servants earning less than that amount so that they will not be subjected to the cut? I would recommend that all other salaries, including those of judges, lieutenant-governors and ministers of the crown, be cut to the extent of the amount they are in excess of $6,000. I do not know if hon. members understand the position I take, but it is this:

I feel that it is well to practise the cut on ourselves, to-show that we are setting a good example. At a later time I may have the opportunity to discuss whether or not any cut is necessary.
Admitting however for the moment that it is necessary, we must adopt the cut ourselves. I do not share the view of the hon. member from Nova Scotia who said that hon. members should not suffer a cut. If such action is to be taken, it should become operative right here in the House of Commons and in the Senate. My idea would be that a cut of ten per cent would be made in salaries ranging between $4,000 and $6,000, and that salaries in excess of $6,000 to all others, including judges, lieutenant-governors, ministers and so on, would be depreciated by the amount they are in excess of $6,000, to compensate for the special consideration given to the poorly paid servants. Would not such an arrangement be fair?
First of all, however, the special allowance given to ministers should be taken away. I was very much surprised a few days ago to learn that the estimates show no cut in that special allowance, and I cannot understand the attitude of the government in that regard. I have to apologize to the house for having made the mistake of saying that the ten per cent cut applied in that particular connection. I wonder if the ministers of the crown have taken the trouble to consult the estimates and see if the allowance is still operative. I should like to remove not only that allowance, but to correct the whole discrimination against members of parliament and others in the civil service of Canada who are suffering from the cut.
At this point I am led to say a few words about the judges. My regard for the bench is high, and I know that at all times that body of men has set an example of self sacrifice. Many outstanding lawyers who were earning high fees in their practice as legal counsel have made sacrifices to go on the bench at lower salaries. Hon. members must have noticed that the judges who came to Ottawa asking the committee then sitting for increases in salary were not all the most prominent figures on the bench. There is one point, however, which has been overlooked by those who have spoken, and it is this: The statement has been made that judges' salaries are statutory. True, but they were also statutory when some years ago they were increased.
I can think of judges who accepted their offices at salaries of $5,000; in the meantime, however, their salaries have risen to $9,000.

May I compliment the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) upon the stand he took concerning a particular case I have in mind. He granted leave to an old judge 83 years of age. That judge was appointed when he was quite old at a salary of $5,000. His superannuation, if taken now would be $6,000, being two-thirds of his regular salary of $9,000. His personal wealth brings him a very substantial annual income. He has not yet resigned. Why? Is the reason that after having completed twenty years on the bench he might receive $1,000 more superannuation? At the same time other judges who are sane in mind and body are overworked. I compliment the Minister of Justice upon forcing the judge to take his leave, but I am sorry a resignation has not been recommended so that he might be succeeded by some other judge, who could do the work.
Judges when appointed to the bench receive certain salaries, which they accept. On account of representations made to the then government judges' salaries were increased; so much the better for them. To-day however we are in different circumstances, and I do not see why the judges would refuse to accept the cut. I am sure no member of the cabinet has received representations from judges to the effect that they would refuse a cut; I am sure neither the Minister of Justice, who holds as high regard for the bench as I do, nor the Prime Minister has received such communication. Then, why not give the people the right impression, and if a cut has to be made adjust it so that those receiving the higher salaries will be affected as much as the low wage earners, Ies gagne-petit, as we call them in French, who have so much trouble in their attempts to make both ends meet.
I wish now to address my remarks to that part of the subject (concerning lieutenant-governors. I have a high respect for those special representatives of the crown in each of the provinces, but I wonder if they are very necessary. In the province of Ontario we have an example where the office of lieutenant-governor, which was vacated a few months ago, is held by the chief justice of the province. A few years ago I addressed a question to the leader of the Labour party (Mr. Woods-worth), who was speaking about curtailments which were to be made, asking him if it would not be feasible to replace lieutenant-governors by the chief justice of each province. Some weeks ago Mr. Georges Pelletier, a former president of the press gallery and a prominent newspaper man wrote in Le Devoir that such

Public Service-Salary Deduction
action should be considered, that a great saving would result to the federal exchequer, the provinces .and the lieutenant-governors themselves. The practice being now followed in Ontario has been tried in other provinces between the death or the dates of resignations of lieutenant-governors and a.ppointments of successors. The duties of a lieutenant-governor are by no means onerous; he has only to sign bills, letters patent and orders in council. For the time being at least I can see no necessity for the appointment of new lieutenant-governors, and believe the chief justice of each province could perform the offices more economically to all concerned. This is a suggestion which I respectfully submit should be considered by the government in due course.
Many generals and officers of the army and navy are chiefly has-beens, and serve no practical purpose at this time. They carry swords and wear what we call full regalia; of course they look very splendid and picturesque but the people derive no benefit from them. Those who should receive as great consideration are the privates, the noncommissioned officers, and the lieutenants who fought under shell-fire in no man's land. Many of them are to-day in the civil service and receiving small salaries. They risked their lives when some generals and other higher officers who receive higher salaries were in the rear. But these fighting men instead of being given that consideration which the nation owes them for their sacrifices at the front in defence of their country, are now penalized to the extent of a ten per cent reduction of their comparatively low salaries, while the generals and other high officers who were safe in their dugouts are still quite safe, they are still away from all danger-their salaries are not cut. It is the man who risked his life in the front line trenches who has to pay for the general who remained safe in his dugout. I submit, Mr. Chairman, that this treatment is most unfair and most unjust.

I wish to conclude the remarks I rose to deliver before the dinner recess. There have been two kinds of exaggerations. The first, in my humble belief, is that according to the resolution the poorly paid civil servants are to suffer a cut, while the other is that a drastic cut is not made in the salaries of those receiving the larger 41761-52
amounts. I would suggest that the government consider the middle course, so that the lower paid and the better paid grades will contribute in a graded proportion. As I said before, many civil servants are returned soldiers who fought in the great war, and they are to suffer a cut. This point has not been mentioned before, although no doubt many hon. members have thought of it. Here a distinction should be made also between parade generals and officers of high rank who had no war service, and others who have performed useful services for this country; there should be a distinction between those who deserve the thanks of the country for the help they gave during trying times and those who have done nothing, who have only a title which they obtained in some way or other.
I should like to make one further observation. It would be wrong for the public to get the impression that members of both houses of parliament are contributing only ten per cent of their indemnity. I suppose the experience of hon. members opposite is the same as my own; when we go to our constituencies we meet people who are needy and who come to us for assistance. We give them a quarter, a half dollar or a dollar; we give them what we can, and we are sorry we cannot give them more. I am sure this has been the experience of hon. members on both sides of the house. Even here in Ottawa, while we are attending our parliamentary duties, when we walk home from the parliament buildings very often we meet people who may be fairly well dressed but who ask us for something to eat, and no one refuses them. This is one kind of assistance that is not mentioned; I refer to it only so that people may have a better understanding of what the members are doing, and may know that we are not neglecting our duties as citizens when we come in contact with unfortunate cases of distress and misery.
Before I resume my speech, Mr. Chairman, I should like to point out that a cut affecting so many people is economically unsound. Economists have told us that in the last few years wealth has been concentrated in the hands of a few; a certain number of men get richer by many thousands of dollars, but that money comes from a great many people, so when we come to a time of depression the purchasing power of these people is naturally lessened. Consider a man who is very rich; even if he spends his money lavishly he cannot eat as many potatoes or as much beef or mutton or bread as ten families can eat; even if he dresses very well and spends a great deal of money on his wardrobe he cannot spend as much as would be required to clothe ten

I bring these matters before the committee in all sincerity, in order to show the government that there are two sides of the question to be considered; it is not at all a matter of party politics. speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Prior to the dinner adjournment the senior member for Ottawa asked me a question which at the moment I was not in a position to answer. The total number of civil servants in receipt of salaries of $1,200 per year or less is 16,408.

I want to ask the minister
two questions, but before doing so I must deprecate very much the acceptance by the chairman this afternoon of a point of order raised by the Minister of Justice. I believe, sir, you accepted his point of order without looking into the authorities, perhaps because no one on the opposition side pointed out where that would lead us. As I understood the point of order raised by the Minister of Justice, it would confine the discussion of this resolution in committee entirely to the terms of the resolution itself. This affords very narrow scope indeed for discussion, and if that is the view held I would ask, what is the use of putting these resolutions into committee of the whole? We have already discussed its principle on the motion to go into committee, and if we are to be confined now strictly to the same subject matter then the committee stage is merely a farce. I understood, and certainly it has always been the practice in the past, that the discussion in committee would be allowed to range, if perhaps not into the details of the bill itself, at any rate into the details of the principle, so to speak, allowing the committee to explore and canvass every angle of the situation as revealed by the resolution in its broad sense. The theory has been, and I can recall occasions when it has been acted upon by the government, that some valuable information might be gleaned from the views expressed by members in the committee and that the government might, in the light of those views, moderate or change the bill which 
would afterwards be brought down. If my memory serves me rightly the government last year did somewhat modify a bill which they were going to introduce, after representations had been made by the opposition while it was in committee of the whole. I notice that in spite of the point of order the debate has been allowed to extend in the usual way all over the subject, but I wish to protest now, not only as regards the matter at present before us but in view of what may happen in the future, against the position that has been taken. It would be very inimical to the best interests of the subject under discussion if it became the practice.
I would point out that May, at page 507, lays down that debate on such a resolution must be confined to the terms of the resolution and must not extend to the bill itself.

Yes; but May is only our
last resort when we do not know what to do ourselves. I think that in these days when precedent is so largely followed I might point to the precedent of a good many years' standing, under which we have been allowed to discuss the subject in its broadest aspect. However, I will confine myself for the moment to the terms of the resolution. It was suggested this afternoon-and this illustrates the need for allowing the fullest range of discussion-that we must not discuss exemptions because they are not mentioned in the resolution. I would point out, however, that in his very first remarks the Minister of Finance mentioned half a dozen exemptions. But in any case an exemption is mentioned in this resolution, because the second paragraph declares that the purpose is to provide for the payment by the government of contributions due under the Civil Service Superannuation Act in respect of those members of the civil service who receive $1,200 or less. That is certainly an exemption and it is upon that point that I wish to base the question I am about to ask. I do not know how many, but there are a large number of civil servants both in Ottawa and outside who are not eligible to pay into the superannuation fund. If I mistake not there are many of them in the Finance department and also in the soldier settlement branch, and I know that in the outside service there are quite a number. I will illustrate by one class that comes into my mind just now. I refer to employees on government fishing patrol boats and boats used in connection with the lighthouse service, and also the men on lifeboats. They get a miserable salary, $65 a month, I believe, sup-

remains, I hope, to be discussed. So far it has not been. That might be so if my
hon. friend was trying to see how ridiculous he could make it. I want to discuss this matter with the resolution before us clearly in mind, and I want to point out to my hon. friend before the bill is introduced just where this is going to lead. This is the inevitable result of taking a ten per cent slash at all salaries without any consideration of where you are going to land. I submit that with the greatest courtesy possible in dealing with a 
resolution as ill-considered as this resolution appears to me to be.
Take the principle of a graduated scale. Is there anybody in this house on either side or in any corner who will deny the equity of that principle? My hon. friend has practically admitted the equity of it by allowing a deduction of five per cent from the man drawing a salary of $1,200 and less. Is not that correct? Why was the deduction of five per cent made in that case instead of ten per cent?-^because that is what it amounts to. The reason was that it was not considered equitable that a man receiving $1,200 or less Should get as high a percentage cut as the man receiving above that figure. There can be no question about that. The $1,200 man is being given consideration because he receives a low salary, and the principle of a graduated scale is admitted when the government pays five per cent towards the superannuation fund in respect of that man's salary. Having started out that way, how on earth can my hon. friend justify leaving the man between $1,200 and $2,000 with' exactly the same percentage of reduction as the man between $6,000 and $8,000? Why not continue to follow the same line of reasoning that my hon. friend apparently has commenced? Why not give to that low salaried man between $1,200 and $2,000 the same consideration you give to the man who is rceiving $1,200 or less? That is what appeals to me very strongly.
I want to say this further to my hon. friend, that so far as I am concerned I opposed this resolution just because I was afraid that the very result would ensue which the Minister of Finance now tells me will follow from its adoption. I opposed it because I believe in a graduated scale of reduction, similar to that in effect with regard to income tax, succession duties, and so on. I submit the proposal now before us is contrary to the practice which has been followed in the various provinces and by the dominion in regard to matters of this kind. My hon. friend may answer, "oh, no''. My reply is however, in the words of the hon. member for Shelburne-Yarmouth (Mr. Ralston), that the proposed cut is not a reduction but really constitutes an impost or tax. If the proposed cut is in the nature of an income tax levy, then are we to understand that to that extent the people affected will not be subjected to income tax? I think we may dismiss any such considerations from our minds, because undoubtedly they will be subjected to the operations of the income tax, just as other people who are receiving salaries.
I want to say also that I am not opposed to the cut, but I think it should be graded.

I am opposed to the exemptions, I do not think they can be justified before the people of Canada. I say frankly to my hon. friend the Minister of Finance that there are a great many people in Canada to-day who are in a much worse position than those civil servants receiving salaries of $1,200. But the greatest indignation will be felt throughout Canada if the high salaried persons are cut to no greater extent than those receiving the smaller salaries. There will be further resentment against certain civil servants who may suffer no cut at all. I think any such arrangement is ill considered, and the minister would do well, when the bill is introduced to try to make up the required revenue by taking a higher percentage from the higher salaries.
I agree that money must be had for the public treasury, and it is the duty of my hon. friend and his colleagues to raise it, a task which is by no means easy. Surely, however, it will be much easier for him and for those associated with him who are charged with the responsibility, to raise the money in a more equitable fashion so that the burden may be placed upon the shoulders of those able to bear it rather than upon the shoulders of the lower paid civil servants.
There are many low salaried people who are finding it difficult to get along without reductions ; and then there are certain classes, I must admit, who are even worse off. Unfortunately the farmers, who receive no salaries at all and who at the present time are getting no returns on their investments, are suffering more than any other people in Canada. Everything they have to buy is priced altogether out of proportion to the amounts they receive for the goods they have to sell. Nevertheless they are not being helped by an injustice perpetrated upon some other class.
I am bound to submit to my hon. friend that a bill such as he has described, which will follow rigidly the terms of the resolution now before us, will be most unjust. When the bill is introduced, if it be found that an amount equal to that anticipated can be raised by instituting cuts on a graduated scale, I submit such changes could be made constitutionally and with the approval of Canadians generally.

May I go back to the

I am prepared to admit that it is a deduction, which in the long run amounts to ten per cent less salary. We are all agreed on that. But the Prime Minister has changed the wording since his declaration in the house. Then he said the salaries would be reduced. That meant that the range of the salaries would be disturbed. But, as I understand, this resolution does not reduce the range; it simply takes ten per cent away from salaries within that range, for this year. Nevertheless it is an arbitrary deduction; you cannot get

away from it. This afternoon the Minister of Finance said there had been some consultation with some representatives of the civil service. But the civil servants apparently were not consulted, because the delegates came to represent thirty-five of the affiliated associations, covering something like 62,000 members of the service. When some time in 1923 or so a reduction was made in the bonus of the civil servants, a consultation took place. We on this side of the house consulted with the civil service. Of course, they objected to having a reduction in the bonus, but they were heard. They presented memoranda, they had interview after interview with the Minister of Finance, to whom I had the pleasure of introducing those deputations. Of course, the cut was made, but only after full consultation with representatives of the civil service. Nothing would have been easier than to have followed the same practice this j'ear. No doubt a ten per cent cut would have been made, but the same result could probably have been arrived at by means of some other arrangement. That is why I say this is a purely arbitrary deduction.
The minister asserts that a straight or horizontal cut is the only way in which to produce equality of treatment. Well, here Is a contrast: a minister of the crown in receipt of 814,000 a year has to pay $1,400; a civil servant who earns $1,200 a year, and does not contribute to the superannuation fund or the retirement fund, will have to pay $120. Surely the minister will not argue for a moment that the $14,000 man is not better able to suffer and bear his reduction in salary than the man who suffers a reduction of $120. The minister sees at once the difficulty. So long as you keep within the high range of salaries the cut is not so felt. He who is in receipt of $21,000 can easily suffer a reduction of $2,100. The Secretary of State (Mr. Cahan) smiles.

I was wondering how often
the hon. member had been -cut in that way.

I have never received
$21,000 a year.
Then why mention it?

Now that the Secretary of State has raised the point, I submit that in the very nature of things I must feel a cut of $400 in my indemnity to a far greater extent than the Prime Minister will feel a cut -of $2,100 on his salary of $21,000, supplemented as it is by his private income. The moment you get to the lower range the pressure is harder. That is why it is so difficult for the lower salaried civil servants to view
this shrinkage in their income with any degree of satisfaction. The Prime Minister said that they ought to be enthusiastic; well, I do not know how they can be expected to become enthusiastic over a loss of $120 on a total salary of $1,200. If this is to be treated purely and simply as a deduction, then why should not the same deduction apply all through? Surely it would not be a breach of contract to apply it as well to the high salaries of the judges and military and naval officers. There is a contract of employment between the civil servant and the crown, or there is not; there is a contract between the judge and the crown, or there is not. There is a contract between the civil servant and the crown in so far as contractual obligations can exist between the crown and its servants. Proof of that is undoubtedly to be found in the statute and in the form of contract used by the Civil Service Commission. The Civil Service Commission advertises these positions; there is the offer and then the acceptance, and that is a binding contract, or I know nothing about it. Just taking an ordinary form circulated by the Civil Service Commission, the offer made by the government through its agent the Civil Service Commission is in these words:
In the event of a permanent appointment the initial salary of $2,280 will be increased-
There is the promise.
*-upon recommendation for efficient service at the rate of $120 per annum until a maximum of $2,700 has been reached.
That is the offer, and the civil servant accepts, so the contract is binding. He is given the position, and under the statute it is ratified. If the Minister of Finance can find a better form of contract, including the offer, the acceptance, the ratification by statute and the binding obligation on the crown to continue to employ that man as long as he fulfils his part of the contract by good conduct, I do not understand anything about the law on contracts. The crown also promises by statute, through the advertisement which is accepted by the applicant, that upon good conduct the civil servant will be entitled to and will be paid a statutory increase.
The contract from which I read was dated November 23, 1931, and so much did the government recognize that it contained a binding contract that in the new form of notice sent out by the Civil Service Commission and dated March 4, 1932, we find these words, offering another contract:
The salary is, however, subject to such temporary reduction or subsequent increase-

Let us hope there will be a subsequent increase, since we are sure there is to be a temporary reduction.
-as may be authorized by parliament.
These are no idle words; there must have been a reason for saying that from and after a certain date there shall be a new form of contract; there must have been a contract previously. I cannot see how the Minister *of Finance, even with his high attainments, can get away from it. But there was a statement made by the Minister of Justice that should not be allowed to go by. The Minister of Justice endeavoured to differentiate between the contract applying to a judge and the contract applying to a civil servant. So far as judges are concerned, the Minister of Justice says they cannot be retired, while if a naval or'military officer wants to retire before his term is up he may be arrested. But the Minister of Justice added, "If terms are imposed upon the civil servants that are unfair, he can resign."
That is a statement which cannot be allowed to go unchallenged. If I understand the Minister of Justice correctly, he means that, obligations being imposed and contractual relation having existed, if unfair terms are imposed what is the remedy? The employee may resign. That is a most extraordinary statement, that the crown may force one of its employees to resign by imposing upon him unfair terms. With all deference to the Minister of Finance I cannot see how he can escape the binding obligation, the contractual relation between the crown and the civil servant.
As I have said, this new contract is dated March 4. 1932. Whoever advised the Civil Service Commission, or whoever cast a legal eye over this contract, knew very much more about it, apparently, than the person who drafted this resolution, because at once they saw the objection that there is this responsibility upon the government to respect the legal relation, the contractual obligation that has been made with the civil servant, in view of the fact that he is entitled to a permanent position at a stated annual or monthly salary, and that such is to continue as long as he conducts himself properly.
In view of that, these people have contracted obligations. The man in the commercial world works from day to day, from week to week, from month to month or has a contract for one year. A man who has a contract for one year may lease an apartment and buy a certain amount of furniture, but he knows that he does so at his own peril, that at the end of that year the contract may be

terminated. When the civil servant accepts a position at a certain salary that is to be paid if he conducts himself properly, with a statutory increase of S60 a year in certain grades and S120 a year in others until he reaches a certain maximum, he cuts his coat according to his cloth. He enters into contractual obligations; he buys a house and puts a mortgage on it; he knows the amount of interest he has to pay; he buys some furniture and makes out his budget so as to enable himself to carry on. Recently the civil servants, of their own good will, contributed to the unemployment relief fund, and the minister paid them a tribute they well deserved. Had they known that, right out of the blue, with no notice whatever, and to take effect immediately, their salaries were to be reduced it might have been a different story. Now they have contracted an obligation which they may find it hard to keep. I cite that just as an example. I have had people come to me and say "This means starvation; I just renewed my lease on the first of February." The house opened on February 4, and they had no premonition that this was to happen. They have renewed old obligations and contracted new ones on this promise to pay; the promise now is shattered, and the contractual relation broken.
If this matter had been approached in a different way it would have been a great deal easier. If the minister had said, "Very well, you as the debtor will be unable to meet your commitments to the extent of ten per cent, so something must be done whereby the creditor will not collect to the extent of ten per cent," matters might have been adjusted, but under present conditions I say this arbitrary action will impose a heavy burden upon those least able to bear it.
I might as well be frank about it; I am absolutely opposed to any cut under these circumstances. I think it is the most unfair thing that could be done. It was done in a most arbitrary way, and will not produce the results anticipated. We may talk of patriotism; it is a very good thing to talk about, but the government and the outside world have no monopoly on patriotism. The civil sendee is patriotic also. But if the farmers and those in other spheres of life feel the effect of this economic situation to-day, there is no reason why someone who is now enjoying a steady income should have that income reduced, when no direct benefit will result to anyone else. If the civil service is cut to this extent it will not bring one cent of relief to the farmers or to mechanics or to the professional classes. It will be just the other way

around; it will reduce by that much the purchasing power of the civil servant. Why should one take the attitude that because a man in business has been mulcted to a certain extent, his business suffering, his income reduced, and himself in financial difficulties, he should on that account begrudge somebody else who is in a more fortunate position? If the government decided to cut these salaries by ten per cent but at the same time to force all employers of labour who reduced by ten per cent the wages and salaries of their employees to contribute that money to the treasury, putting it alongside the $8,000,000 which it is expected to raise from the reduction in civil service salaries, then I am quite satisfied that the civil service would never have been heard from. But I do think that it is a most unfair and inequitable thing to force the civil servants of Canada to contribute $8,000,000 to the national exchequer when the people outside will not contribute one cent. If the employer of labour turned into the coffers of the state whatever reductions in salaries he might make so far as his own employees are concerned, then there would be an excuse for it; but instead of going into the national exchequer side by side with the moneys which will be taken from the civil servants it will simply be used for the purposes of those who cut salaries outside. Those reductions will be used for the benefit of their own businesses and they will not help one bit the reduction of the national debt. Tor these reasons I cannot support this resolution at all. I make this distinction so far as indemnities are concerned:	When I vote against
the reduction I am not voting against the reduction in the indemnities of members of parliament.

I wish to make clear
the position which I have taken in this matter. Generally speaking, I may say that, as I voted, I am in favour of the general principle of a reasonable cut. I have felt for some time, and so I believe have many other people in the country, that there is one class of people who have been exempt and entirely protected from the effects of the depression, and the depression can always be borne more easily the wider the foundation on which it rests. For that reason I supported the resolution. But there are certain objections which I have to the details of the cut, first in respect to the lower salaries. I shall not dwell on that because it has been discussed at great length, but I do think that the system of gradation should have been carried to a greater extent than it has been. My objection to some of the details applies,
however, more particularly to the anticipated exemptions.
It has been suggested that we are somewhat premature, if not out of order, in discussing exemptions at the present time, in that they are not specifically mentioned in the terms of the resolution. I cannot agree with that, because in voting on the general principle we must, if we are to vote intelligently, have some conception of the character of the cut-how wide-embracing it may be, how complete, what the exemptions will be, to what extent they will go, and so on. All that must be embodied in the principle itself, and I think those questions might fairly be discussed in discussing the principle. Coming to the exemptions-and there are several exemptions-I shall take first the Department of National Defence and kindred branches. It has been pointed out by the Minister of Justice, I believe, that the enlisted men occupy, by reason of their obligations and the obligations of the government to them, a position different from that of the ordinary civil servant; the terms of their enlistment are more strict and they have not the same freedom of action. That, I think, is a fair argument. But does it apply to the administrative officials of the department, that is, to the deputy minister and his staff and other officials not enlisted men?
Those are all cut.
No, they are not cut.
Yes, the deputy minister and the others.

Then I withdraw the
objection so far as that goes. I come then to my chief objection and that is the exemption of judges. It is largely a matter of principle, but may I ask this:	In what
different position does the judge find himself from, say, the railway commissioners, the pension commissioners or members of other commissions of that sort, all of whom suffer the cut? They also are definitely appointed under statute; their salaries are just as definitely fixed by statute as those of the judiciary. It has been said year after year, and I think correctly, that these commissioners to whom I refer occupy judicial positions, that their work is of a judicial character, that their responsibilities are judicial, and that in every respect they are comparable to judges on the bench or the ordinary judges in different parts of the country. Now I ask, why should one class of judges be exempt while the other class receive these cuts? It is something that does not appeal to my sense of justice.

I supported the resolution because I believe in the general principle that all citizens should bear their fair share of the weight of depression. Nor do I take seriously for a moment the argument that we are reducing purchasing power by the cut in these salaries. That would be true if it applied to reduction of wages in ordinary life, but not where these wages are derived from taxation. It is a question of distribution rather than a reduction of purchasing power. It will reduce purchasing power in Ottawa, but it does not reduce purchasing power in the country generally. Every dollar that comes into the city of Ottawa by way of salary must be taken from the purchasing power of those in other parts of the country, so that I do not take that objection seriously. But I do take most seriously the suggested exemption of judges. How can that be justified in view of the fact that the members of these commissions I have mentioned, paid under statute, performing judicial services under statute, are subject to the reduction?

Let me make this further comment, which is only in connection with county court judges -and I say this not in any critical way, for I have every respect for the judiciary; I think the judiciary of the Dominion of Canada stands as high as that of any other country in the world.
