speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
Notwithstanding the discussion of this resolution in the house when we thought we had succeeded in converting my hon. friend, when the vote came we found we were wrong and we missed his vote. He was not in the chamber when the vote was taken.
I do not know how serious he is in the questions he has asked; at all events I can regard them as having been seriously put and will state my views in a serious manner in regard to the matters he has mentioned. Of all branches of the administration of government in this or any other country I believe the most important is that of the administration of justice. You may pass in this parliament what laws you see fit, but unless those laws are fairly and honestly administered by a competent judiciary the results will not be satisfactory. The men, regarding whom the greatest caution should be exercised and the greatest consideration had, are those who from time to time are appointed to the bench in the various courts throughout the dominion. We approach a man who we think is qualified from his standing in the community, his general reputation, and especially his legal knowledge and ability, and invite him to accept a seat upon the bench. If he does so he is to a very large extent removed from the ordinary affairs, conditions and circumstances of life, to such an extent indeed that in many cases he has to forego former friendships and former associations. He has to give up the practice of his profession and he must not engage in any kind of business whatsoever. He may be a man who has enjoyed a highly lucrative legal practice. He goes upon the bench with a distinct understanding as to what he is to receive by way of salary and as to the tenure of his term of office. He knows that he cannot be removed through the device or whim of any person or through any political consideration. He is absolutely independent in his judicial position

Public Service-Salary Deduction
and we desire to keep him so. A judge's salary is fixed by statute and provision is made for his ultimate retirement. In the ease of county judges to whom reference has been made by my hon. friend, after thirty years' service on the bench, which is a long term of service, a county court judge may retire on full pay. It has been said that they may retire at any time. That is true, and the pension payable to them upon retirement is fixed according to the number of years they have served, provided they have served a minimum of five or ten years. But if they should retire, what can they do? They are out of practice, their clients and their business have disappeared. They have added five or ten years to their lives, and their chances of making a livelihood under those circumstances are very slim indeed. I submit that if we are going to maintain the high character of the judiciary of this country, as it has been maintained in the past, we must pay our judges substantial salaries and assure them in regard to the permanency of their positions; and we must also make provision for their ultimate retirement. Otherwise we will not secure the eminent class of men that we desire to see upon the bench in this country. Speaking generally, we have enjoyed in Canada since confederation, a very able, upright and distinguished body of men in the various courts in Canada, but there have been, I am sorry to say some exceptions. We strive to get the ablest and best qualified men we can for the modest salaries which we are able to pay as authorized by this parliament.
With regard to county judges, I may say that $5,000 is the salary of a county or a district judge. We have county or district judges in all provinces of 'Canada save in the province of Quebec, where they maintain a different judicial system from the other provinces of the dominion. This government does not establish the various courts of the provinces or the number of judges in the provinces. When my hon. friend says that there is a slight increase in the estimates of the Department of Justice this year, it is true there is an increase of between $4,000 and $5,000, but this increase has arisen because the provinces, by legislation, have requested us to appoint four additional county court judges. Otherwise there would have been from $16,000 to $17,000 of a reduction. But in compliance with the request of the provinces four additional county judges were appointed at $5,000 apiece. That is the reason for the apparent increase. Otherwise there would have been a reasonable decrease in the estimates of the Department of Justice.
I know that in Great Britain the salaries of judges were decreased last autumn, and

that was done I understand with the consent of the judges themselves, or of a number of them. Judges' salaries in Great Britain and in Australia and South Africa are much higher than in the Dominion of Canada. Whether they are able in this way to secure better or abler judges in Australia and South-Africa than we do in Canada I cannot say, but this I can say, that the salaries we now pay as authorized by this parliament do not attract many of the men whom we would like to elevate to the bench of this country. Man after man has replied to our invitation to consider a seat upon the bench that he cannot afford to do so having regard to the salary he would receive as a judge and the amount of the emolument which he annually receives from his practice. With only $15,000 as the salary of the chief justice of the Dominion of Canada, which is the highest judicial post in this country, we cannot hope to attract the greatest and most distinguished lawyers in this dominion. We have to do the best we can under the circumstances. If you have only nine or ten thousand dollars to offer for a position on the bench, all you can expect to secure is a nine or ten thousand dollar man. You cannot get an oustanding man in the profession for that salary. I am one of those who believe that the time has already passed when this house should consider the revision upwards of judicial salaries in Canada. I do not say that in respect of all our courts, but I do say it in respect of our higher courts. This I realize would not be an opportune time to suggest such an increase, but in years past I have had a very strong opinion that the salaries of judges in our higher courts should be materially increased. We recall that a committee of this house was appointed to consider this matter two or three years ago. That committee did not report favourably in regard to increases in judicial salaries. Some other consideration, sessional indemnities or something of the kind, became involved in the deliberations of that committee, and no favourable recommendation was made at that time. But I believe the day is not far distant when we shall have to revise upwards the salaries paid to some of the judges of our higher courts if we are going to continue to insist upon securing the ablest and best qualified men to administer the laws * of this country. I believe that the administration of the law is a more important branch of the government of a country than the executive authority which is vested in the government. If our laws are properly administered, fairly and honestly administered,, we have gone a long way in the government

of our country. But if our law is not fairly and fully administered, then our decline is not very far distant. For myself may I say that I do not think it would be proper to reduce the salary of a judge without his consent under the circumstances under which he has been appointed.

This is not a
reduction in salary.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Well then this deduction, or whatever my right hon. friend chooses to call it-this ten per cent cut which is proposed in the present resolution. Have I made myself clear now? I do not think that judicial salaries should be subjected to the proposed ten per cent reduction. It has been suggested to me that it might not be constitutional to attempt it. That is a debatable point. The judges of some of our courts are appointed directly under the authority of the British North America Act. The judges in other courts are appointed under authority of the statutes of this parliament. It may be that something may be urged against the constitutionality of such a proposal in respect to those judges who are appointed under the British North America Act, while other considerations might be involved in the case of judges who are appointed under the authority of acts of this parliament. Our county court judges, our supreme court judges, our exchequer court judges have all been appointed under the authority of our own acts. Not so however in the case of the superior courts of the provinces of Canada which existed at the time of confederation and have since been continued. The judges of those courts were appointed pursuant to a section of the British North America Act, and a serious question might arise as to the constitutionality of any act we might pass with regard to them.
Under the section of the British North America Act by which these judges were appointed, is the salary set?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
The salary is not set by the British North America Act, but was set by this parliament. The British North America Act provides that we shall appoint the judges, pay their salaries and allowances. In that connection a point occurs to me which may be discussed when we proceed, a few days hence, with a bill to amend the Judges' Act. I question whether the Dominion of Canada should be called upon to pay the ordinary travelling expenses of the judges in Canada, although we have done so since confederation. The provinces administer the law in the provinces, and the judges are responsible for that administration, but we have been in
the habit of paying the expenses of judges travelling throughout their own counties in the administration of provincial laws. That is a question however for future discussion. We have always paid these travelling expenses because the word "allowance" occurs in the British North America Act. There is a strong opinion however that the word "allowance" refers to a retiring allowance or a leave allowance. If it were intended that we should pay travelling expenses undoubtedly the words "travelling expenses" would have been inserted in the act. However, that is not the question now before us.
For the reasons I have already stated, personally I am opposed to the ten per cent cut in judges salaries, but I agree we have a right to tax those salaries should we see fit to do so. We did so when we imposed the income tax.

Without amending the
constitution?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: A question as to the constitutionality of our action was raised, and a decision was given by the Judicial Committee of the Privy Council in favour of the right of this parliament to tax judges' salaries. While I do not think we could properly subject judges' salaries to this ten per cent reduction, I will say that, it is entirely within our power to subject them to a ten per cent tax. That is the distinction I draw between the two. I do not want to interfere with the solemn contracts we made with those men when they were appointed to the bench. I desire to keep judicial appointments entirely free from influence or threats. I want judges to feel absolutely secure in the positions they hold; I want them to administer the laws of this country without fear or favour from any quarter or section, and I desire that they receive sufficient salaries and emoluments to make them absolutely independent of any influence whatsoever. If we continue to maintain proper conditions we will secure proper and just administration 'of our laws. Such is the way in which a high standard of administration of the law has been secured in Great Britain. In that country exceedingly high salaries are paid to judges, and I believe judges there have themselves agreed to a very substantial reduction in their salaries. That of course is a matter of agreement. Salaries of judges in Great Britain are sufficiently high to attract many of the ablest men at the bar in England. We must also consider the security of the position, as well as the substantial salaries and the care taken upon retirement. I consider judicial posi-

tions in Canada as something distinct entirely from ordinary positions under the government. We have always endeavored to treat them as distinct; the country in general respects its judiciary very highly and I would not be one to interfere lightly with salaries which we are pledged to pay.

I believe the minister
was regretting the inadequacy of the remuneration which rendered it almost impossible to bring to the bench the services of the most outstanding lawyers at the bar. The suggestion, which seems to have some merit, has been made to me-and I am speaking only as a layman-that the qualities in a lawyer which tend to make him most successful in private practice, from a financial point of view, are not necessarily the qualities which would make him the best judge. That is, the impartial, judicial qualities which are so essential in a judge, and without which a judge cannot be most effective, are not always found in the most successful lawyers. Naturally however some qualities of the successful judge are found in the most successful lawyers pleading at the bar. Would the minister tell me if there is anything in that point, and if we are still able to secure men who, though admirably adapted to judicial duties, have not been the most successful in, private practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext:
There may be something in the suggestion my hon. friend has made. I have known lawyers who were not very highly regarded at the bar, but who were enormously successful in certain lines of legal practice which, one might say, was not of the highest type. Such however are not the men we seek to put upon the bench. We have to look for men of undoubted integrity, men who hold the respect of the communities in which they live, men whose knowledge of the law is undoubted, and men who bear unblemished character. While my hon. friend has suggested that there have been long lists of applicants, for judicial positions, may I say to him that during the year and a half that I have been in the Department of Justice that has not been the case. I have found it very, very difficult to secure the most suitable men for the higher courts in Canada at the salaries which we now pay. I have received many refusals from men I have asked to consider judicial appointments. I think perhaps that does not apply in as great a degree to the county courts as it does to the higher courts. There is not the same difficulty in securing excellent men to accept county court judgeships. But to secure the services of out-

standing men in the legal profession to fill the higher court vacancies has, in my experience of the last eighteen months, not been the easiest matter.

I think the minister
did not grasp fully the import of my question. When I referred to lawyers who were eminently successful in higher practice but did not possess the judicial qualities necessary in judges I was not reflecting upon the character or integrity of those men, but was rather referring to the fact that their abilities may have been confined to those which enabled them to succeed in certain branches of law. Yet that fine judicial or impartial quality which sometimes is detrimental to lawyers is an essential in judicial practice.

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: We try of course to secure broadminded men not only with a knowledge of the customs of the country, and a wide knowledge of law, but who have engaged in general legal practice. I agree that men who have specialized in one line of legal work may not prove to be the best judges. We seek to secure our judges however from men who are accustomed to appear before the courts, who have enjoyed varied practice in our provinces, and men whose character and integrity is undoubted. Forty years ago in Canada, at the salaries then offered, which were much lower than they are now, it was not so difficult to attract leading lawyers to the bench. I can assure the committee however that it is much more difficult to-day owing to the very modest salaries which we pay to judges in this country.

Replying to the Minister of Justice, I should like to say that he has not been fair to me so far as the vote this afternoon was concerned. I was not in the chamber when the vote was taken; had I been here I would have voted for the resolution, and I so placed myself on record a week ago to-night. I said I was not opposed to the ten per cent cut, and the minister was not fair to-day when he insinuated that I ducked the vote. I want to tell him that while I have not been in this parliament as long as he has, and with all due respect for his experience and years in the house, he cannot charge me with ducking a vote since I have been here.
The minister said he thought there was no use replying to me as he could not convert me. I admit at once, Mr. Chairman, that he can never convert me. Let me refer him to his own chief. Speaking in his own city of Guelph some time ago, and on the same

platform with his chief lieutenant, the right hon. Prime Minister stated that he "never had any use for converts, because you could never trust them." I do not presume to say the right hon. gentleman was referring to the hon. member for South Wellington (Mr. Guthrie) when he made that statement.
In dealing with the exemption of judges' salaries from the ten per cent cut, although the Minister of Justice did refer to the matter of contract before he sat down, he based his whole argument on the presumption that the judges do not have enough to live on, that they made great sacrifices when they were elevated to the bench. In fact he went so far as to say that the integrity of these men depend on the salaries they get. I have always understood that when a lawyer accepts a judgeship he does so because his professional standing enables him to serve his country. A few nights ago I referred to the exemption of the army officers from the operation of this ten per cent reduction in salary, and my good friend from Antigonish-Guysborough (Mr. Duff) referred to them this afternoon. I think he put the case very clearly before the committee. If we have any class of civil servants that are overpaid and underworked-my friend says "useless," but I will not go so far as that-they are the army officers attached to the permanent force, not only at headquarters in the city of Ottawa but in every military district in the dominion. It is true they are not very large in numbers, perhaps between 150 and 200, but the average pay drawn by each of those men ranges between $6,000 and $7,000 a year, with free house and found, as we used to say in the old days. My hon. friend says "beer."
In the officers' mess.

I prefer to leave that out of the discussion. But they are well paid. As a matter of fact in comparison with ninety-five per cent of the civil servants living in the city of Ottawa or those outside Ottawa they are much better paid. But there is another feature to be taken into account: these men draw large pensions when they retire, pensions running anywhere from $5,000 up to $7,000 a year, but they do not contribute a single solitary cent to the retirement fund. I am told my information is not correct; if so, I will withdraw that statement. May I ask the Minister of Finance if the army officers of the permanent force pay anything into the superannuation fund?

speakerposition: Minister of Justice and Attorney General of Canada
speechtext: Yes, they do.

Then I am sorry, Mr. Chairman, to have stated to the contrary. My information is wrong. But that does not hurt my case a particle. I say they are overpaid for the work they do. Perhaps those men do more loafing and more swanking and more parading and less work than any other body of men in the service of the crown. But, oh no! you must not cut their salaries. Why should they be exempt? No reason has ever been given why they should not participate in this salary reduction. I do not think any reason can be given for their exemption. I would urge on the Minister of Finance that he go into the pay and allowances of these army officers, that he check up on the amount of work they do-or rather on the amount of work they do not do-and include their salaries in the ten per cent cut.
Then the Royal Canadian Mounted Police apparently are not to be subject to this ten per cent cut. I see no reason why they should be exempt. The Royal Canadian Mounted Police have done credit to Canada all down through the years, the reputation of the force extends all over the world, their record of personal sacrifice and fidelity to duty is perhaps unequalled by any similar force in the world. But I am inclined to think that the members of the Royal Canadian Mounted Police are ready to bear their share of the ten per cent cut. Why should they be exempt? Then there are the lieutenant-governors. I did a little figuring to-night, and I can tell the Minister of Finance that he can save $8,000 or $9,000 a year by making a ten per cent cut in the salaries of these gentlemen. Nobody would object to such a reduction; I doubt even if the lieutenant-governors themselves would demur. Men of the type who become lieutenant-governors accept the position because they have the financial resources to enable them to maintain the social traditions of their office.
About an hour ago the Minister of Finance went so far as to say that perhaps the question of exemptions would be further considered. I would ask him to reconsider them carefully. One of my hon. friends says "prayerfully," and as I look on the minister I think he is a man of prayer. So I hope he will reconsider these exemptions carefully and prayerfully. I plead with him to make no exemptions, to treat all civil servants alike in regard to this ten per cent cut. I need not refer to the condition of the farming industry and to the plight of the unemployed, but I tell the government that this is a time

speechtext: I am very glad my hon. friend has brought that to my attention, because while in London last autumn I heard that many of the judges did not object to the reduction. But what he has stated is no doubt correct.

Mr. Chairman, there is one matter which my hon. friend from Ottawa (Mr. Chevrier) referred to that I think may have left a wrong impression on the house, although of course, this was unintentional on his part. A reference to section 12 of the Civil Service Act will show how the matter of compensation is dealt with. Section 12 says:
The commission shall, from time to time, as may be necessary, recommend rates of compensation for any new classes that may be established hereunder, and may propose changes in the rates of compensation for existing classes.
2.	In each class there shall be a minimum and a maximum salary rate and such intermediate rates as may be considered necessary and proper to provide increases between the minimum and maximum.
3.	Such proposed rates of compensation shall become operative only upon their approval by the governor in council, and, where any increased expenditure will result therefrom, when parliament has provided the money required for such increased expenditure.
But recommendations have not been submitted by the Civil Service Commission in connection with this cut.
I am not dealing with that. I am saying that any rate fixed or any increase proposed or recommended by the commission is operative only when approved by the governor in council.
They have to propose it.
I am dealing with conditions year by year, and over periods of years. According to the express terms of the contract those payments are dependent upon the annual vote of parliament for that purpose.
That refers to an increase, not a reduction.

That refers to the entire payment on account of the civil service of this country. I have before me a copy of the estimates for the year ending March 31, 1932, which shows the amount to be voted, and entirely conditional upon the vote of parliament, to be $12,673,104 while the amount in the estimates authorized by statute was only $358,666. Under the statute there can be no contract outstanding with a civil servant where the salary is not fixed by statute, which in law-I am not discussing morals-is binding until the actual vote is made for that purpose year by year. The salaries are fixed by the Civil Service Commission, but such compensation has no legal effect whatever unless year by year there is placed in the estimates a sum to cover the total amount to be voted for the civil service, and until that amount has been voted.
Then could the salaries of civil servants be changed year by year, up or down?

If parliament in any year does not choose to vote salaries for any class of civil servants, they receive nothing and in law they can claim nothing, because their salaries depend entirely upon the discretion of parliament as exercised year by year.
They can leave the service, and in that way you would cut down the staff.

Quite so; they may go out of the service, but I am dealing with this other question. My hon. friend from Ottawa suggested that there was a fixed contract. He did not use that term, but that was the impression I thought might be left upon the minds of hon. members, whereas in fact there is no fixed contract, as there is in the case of judges. There is no such fixed contract with the civil servant.
What would happen if the salaries of judges were not voted?
The salaries of judges are not. voted annually by this house.
Yes they are.

No, they are not; they are statutory and not voted year by year. In the estimates for last year, under administration of justice, there appeared the sum of $2,124,300 representing the salaries of the judges of this country, which are not voted year by year by this house but which are fixed by

statute. The payment of those sums out of the consolidated revenue fund does not depend year by year upon the vote of this house. Judges are in an entirely different position from members of the civil service whose salaries are always dependent and contingent upon the vote of this house from year to year.
Are not the civil service salaries contingent upon the vote of this house year by year because of the fact that there is a minimum and a maximum?

No, that is not it; the entire amount, minimum or maximum, is so dependent. I do not think there is any doubt about that, and I make that reference in order to distinguish between the conditions under which the salaries of civil servants are paid, and the conditions under which the salaries of judges are paid. I am dealing with the whole body of civil servants. There may be some of them who have salaries fixed by statute, but they must be very few indeed because in the whole civil government estimates there is only $358,660 appropriated by statute for such salaries.
May I point out that it made no difference in England, under the economy act?
I am not an expert on the economy act; I have not read it and I do not know what are the powers of His Majesty in council under it. Therefore I do not propose to discuss it.
The hon. gentleman knows that the salaries of judges were fixed under the Act of Settlement, and that this was abrogated by order in council.

It could be abrogated by order in council only if the parliament of Great Britain, which is supreme in the exercise of its discretion, definitely and specifically authorized His Majesty in council to do so by order in council.
The question of statute or contract did not stop them.

Quite so, but if you wish to deal with the matter under our constitution you cannot do it as we have dealt with the civil service salaries, which depend from year to year upon an annual vote. In order to make this deduction from the salaries of judges it would require a specific amendment to the Judges Act, specifically deducting from 41761-53i
their salaries a certain amount, or reducing their salaries by a certain sum. In the estimates for this year we cannot deal with judges' salaries in that way. We can reduce the amount voted for the civil service of this country, but in doing so we are not violating any contract with any civil servant. I am quite clear as to that.

May I just take up that
point with my hon. friend? As I understand his argument, it is based on page 10 of the estimates on which the salaries authorized by statute are set forth, and my hon. friend states that these salaries cannot be reduced except by a special act of parliament. Have I understood his argument correctly so far, that salaries authorized by statute, namely those of the Governor General, the High Commissioner for Canada in London, the Lieutenant-Governor of Ontario, and so on, can be dealt with only in that way? That is to say, to back up his argument that this obligation to the judges is a statutory, contractual obligation my hon. friend points to the estimates? Allow me to point out to him that one of the bodies not exempt under the terms of this resolution, so far as I know-I am sure it is not exempt-is the Civil Service Commission. Anyone who knows what I have had to say in this house with respect to the Civil Service Commission knows that I am the last one to defend it. But I will say that if an injustice would be committed to the judges in asking them for this forced voluntary contribution, just as great an injustice would be committed to the Civil Service Commishsion, because they are listed as amongst those whose salaries are statutory. They are so listed in the estimates. Moreover, reading the Civil Service Act I find that:
There shall be a commission called the Civil Service Commission, consisting of not more than three members appointed by the governor in council.
And what is their tenure of office?

Each subsequently appointed commissioner shall hold office during good behaviour for a period of ten years from the date of his appointment, save that his tenure of office shall cease upon his attaining the age of sixty-five years. . . . There shall be paid out of the consolidated revenue fund of Canada, to the chairman, a salary of seven thousand dollars, and to each of the other commissioners a salary of six thousand dollars per annum.
There, if anywhere, is a straight contract between the members of the Civil Service

Commission and the government of Canada, ratified and confirmed by statute of this parliament, providing that the chairman shall receive the sum of seventy thousand dollars during the course of ten years.
Who denies it?

Then why do hon. gentlemen opposite, why does the Minister of Justice, why does the Secretary of State, why does the Minister of Finance come to us and say, "We cannot reduce the salaries of judges because forsooth their salaries are guaranteed by statute," when there is a far greater guarantee by statute to the members of the Civil Service Commission whose salaries we are reducing. We want hon. gentlemen opposite to be fair.

There is nothing in this
resolution reducing them.

But there is in the estimate. The position is worse than ever. We were informed by the Minister of Finance this afternoon that certain persons were exempt, namely, judges, officers in the army and navy, representatives of the crown and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police. The estimates show the salaries of the civil service commissioners: one at $6,300 and two at $5,400, making a total of $17,100. By statute of the parliament of Canada, by the law of this dominion, there is a contract between those commissioners, for whom I have no love, and this country, a contract which provides that their salaries shall be, in one instance, $7,000 and not $6,300, and in the other instance $6,000 and not $5,400. I suggest to the Secretary of State that he had better follow the example of the Minister of Justice who, during the whole course of his remarks a few minutes ago, departed altogether from the contractual obligation theory and based his plea in favour of the judges upon the ground of propriety.

I was not making any
argument with regard to the judges.. I was simply pointing out to my learned friend the hon. member for Ottawa (Mr. Chewier) that there was a distinction as regards civil servants whose salaries are contingent upon a vote of this house. If my hon. friend wishes to take up the case of the members of the Civil Service Commission on the ground that their salaries are statutory, which they certainly are according to the section he has read, that is a matter which will fairly come up when the proposals contained in the bill are under discussion.	*

The whole argument we
have heard all day is now discarded, that the judges were in a different position from everyone else because there was a contractual obligation confirmed by statute. If my hon. friend will read the Judges Act he will see that our obligation towards the judges is not as great as our obligation to the Civil Service Commissioners. What do we provide in the Judges Act? There is the following provision:
The Supreme Court of Canada
The salaries of the judges of the Supreme Court of Canada shall be as follows:
Per annum
(a) The Chief Justice of Canada. $15,000
(ib) Six puisne judges, each ....	12,000
Their salaries are provided for only for one year, whereas the civil service commissioners are provided for for ten years, and we are obligated to pay those salaries. Each one of those commissioners, were it not for certain prerogatives of the crown, could go into any court in the land, he could go into any court if he had such a contract with a private concern and sue under it and collect. I may tell my hon. friend something while I am on this subject. In my own city of Quebec we have a body known as the Quebec Harbour Commission, and since the hon. gentleman's friends came into office they have taken it upon themselves to dismiss a certain number of people for what they called political reasons, but merely because we had hearkened to the cry of the hungry and helpless and appointed them under the harbour commission. The firm of which I am a member took forty cases of that kind before the courts of the province of Quebec for wrongful dismissal, dismissal without notice, and were enabled to collect on behalf of these poor people something like $15,000 which the treasury of this country paid. Now if this government were amenable to the ordinary laws of the land they also would be obliged to pay the salaries of the civil service commissioners.
I return now to the argument advanced by the Minister of Justice with regard to propriety. Every phrase he used in urging upon us not to reduce the salaries of the judges was in direct contradiction of the contractual theory of his honourable friend the Minister of Finance. He urged upon us not to reduce the salaries of the judges because it was very difficult to obtain good men to fill these positions. I agree with him. I am not one of those who think the judges' salaries should be reduced, particularly. But they of all people, if they are patriotic, if they have a

Public Service-Salary Deduction
love of country, if they are -men of standing as the Minister of Justice says and as I believe, should be the first to make a -temporary contribution. We are speaking now on the basis of a temporary contribution; we are not speaking on the basis of finding men to fill the position. We are asking these honourable and estimable men who hold these positions to join with their fellow citizens, those who receive lower salaries, in making a contribution to pay for the cost of government. And they should not be denied that privilege. Every argument which my hon. friend used in support of his case for the judges, the argument, for example, that they had to withdraw from other business, that they are set apart, so to speak, can with equal justice be urged on behalf of the railway commissioners of -Canada who, even though their names are not amongst those entitled to exemption, are entitled to salary under an act of -the parliament of this country. Every one of those arguments -can be urged on behalf of the Board of Pension Commissioners, on behalf of the members appointed to -the .pension tribunal, and on behalf of the pension appeal board. Not a word is said by the Minister of Justice which does not apply equally to these, and perhaps a little more so in the case of those appointed to the pension appeal court and the other courts dealing with soldier problems; because during the time they occupy these positions they cannot possibly practise any other profession. In the course of time, at the end of ten years, if they are obliged to vacate these positions, -they will find themselves without anything whatever with which to face the world. If there is one position more than another that should be exempt it is that of the pension tribunal and the pension appeal court. The members of these bodies are obliged to devote themselves to a very special category of -cases dealing with a very special kind of legislation. They are unable to form any connection which will be of use to them when they retire, and they should be protected at least to the extent that their salaries be not reduced any more than those of the judges.
I again urge upon the ministers that their contention as to statutory obligation is not sound either as to theory or practice, and that the argument of propriety applies equally to other public officers and representatives of the crown as -to judges. I urge upon the Minister of Finance, before he introduces his bill, to consider carefully whether, if there is to be a sacrifice, it should not be general and apply to all -classes of the community.

Just along the lines of the argument of the hon. member for Quebec South, I think the Minister of Justice and my good friend the Secretary of State told us that the judges were in a different position from members of the civil service because the former had contractual rights and their salaries were authorized by statute and did not have to be voted, whereas those of the civil service as a whole had to be voted by parliament.
I was dealing with -civil service employees.

Yes. I understood the Secretary of State to say that the salaries of civil service employees had to be voted by parliament, and if parliament so desired it did not need to vote them at all, but the judges' salaries were authorized by statute and consequently -had to be paid whether we voted them or not. In this country there is another dlass whose salaries do not have to be voted by parliament This is the class of which I spoke this afternoon. The salary of the Speaker of the house does not have to be voted by parliament; it is authorized by statute. Will the Secretary of State, who is a great constitutional lawyer, please look at page 15 of the estimates for 1933? On that page the amount to be voted is given as $897,934.40; there is authorized by statute $1,270,000, making a total of $2,167,934.40. The items which I intend to read are authorized by statute and do not have to be voted by the house; yet the government-and I presume the Secretary of State is just as guilty as any other members of the cabinet- in spite of the fact that these votes are authorized by statute, deliberately by order in council or by vote of the -council or by some other means decided to cut the salary of the Speaker of the house from $6,000 to $5,400.

Will the hon. -member allow an interruption? May I call his attention to the fact that on page 15 certain salaries are marked with an -asterisk and a note at the foot reads:
These reductions will be authorized by legislation.

That does not make any difference. It is true there is a footnote saying that these reductions will be authorized by legislation. Why is there not a similar footnote in regard to the salaries of the judges?

Where there is a salary fixed definitely by statute, a reduction in that salary must be by legislation. In the case of civil service employees, where no statutory salary

is fixed, a reduction may legally be made at any session by a reduction in the vote of this parliament. The Minister of Justice has given his reasons why a reduction has not been made in the salaries of judges.
_ Mr- DUFF: My hon. friend must think he is in the police court, -not in parliament.
I will say to my hon. friend that if I were in the police court, I would have a more intelligent audience than now in addressing my hon. friend.
Does that apply all round?

Does that apply to my hon. friends on his side of the house? My argument is this: if the government in their wisdom can make this footnote on page 15 and deduct $600 from the salary of the Speaker of the Senate; if they can deduct $38,400 from the indemnity to senators, which is statutory and is not voted by parliament; if they can deduct $600 from the salary of the Speaker of the house; if they can deduct $400 from the salary of the deputy speaker of the house; if they can deduct $90,000, Mr. Chairman, from the poor and small amount, that we get for our sessional indemnity, then with respect to the judges they should pass the same legislation, about which the Secretary of State speaks, as they do with regard to members of parliament. My hon. friend's argument falls to the ground, I say without fear of contradiction that everybody in the country shall be treated alike. I hate to see my hon. friend lose his $1,400; it is not fair that he should lose it any more than that I should lose my $400. I am opposed to this reduction. My hon. friend was ejected in his constituency on the understanding that he was to receive a sessional indemnity of $4,000. He was taken into the cabinet with a contract, either verbal or otherwise, that for his services he was to receive $10,000 as a minister of the crown.
It is fixed by statute.
Yes, and I say it is a shame that my hon. friend has to accept $1,400 less than he is entitled to from the people of this country.

The Secretary of State has not submitted anything new. He and I have solved many a riddle before and this is no worse than others. I never said that the salary of the civil servant was statutory;
I said that it was a contract. When my hon. friend reads the act, he does not say anything new. The act says: "for existing classes", and the Secretary of State well knows that when those classes are changed, the civil ser-
'Mr. Cahan.]
vant does not suffer a reduction of his salary but continues in that class until the end of his term. Then the new incumbent takes the position subject to a reduction. There is a contract that the new incumbent shall accept the position at the reduced remuneration. There is no power either in the Civil Service Commission or in this parliament to decrease the remuneration while that incumbent is there, and the fact that these amounts are voted yearly does not detract at all from the contract. This parliament could not anticipate and say in one year we will vote hundreds of millions of dollars to pay what has been contracted for when these civil servants entered into the service of the state. The hon. Secretary of State has not in any way met the situation by citing the Civil Service Act. There is no change there at all.

Except that the contract is
conditional upon parliament voting the money from year to year.

Parliament votes the
money as a result of contractual obligation.
No. The obligation is conditional.

I would like to say a
few words in connection with this phase of the resolution. It is amazing to me that a government that makes any pretensions at all to follow democratic principles should take such a course as this government is following in regard to the proposed exemptions. I listened to the leader of the opposition today making a case for a graduated reduction in civil service salaries, and I listened to the reply of the Minister of Finance, who asked with a large gesture; Do you want to make the civil service a preferred class? Here in these exemptions we have a preferred class. The judges are the highest paid servants of the state, and they are not necessarily the most useful part of the service. We are being asked for equal sacrifices. Is it equal sacrifice to make a deduction of ten per cent from the salary of a man receiving only eight or twelve hundred dollars a year-and there are large numbers in the civil service in that class-while those who are getting salaries ranging up to $15,000 are exempt? Is that equality of sacrifice?
However, the point I wish to make is this: There is always a reason why people do things. The reason brought forward by the government for making the reductions is that the country is in difficulties and they desire each one to contribute his share in order to help balance the budget. But does it not seem

Public Service-Salary Deduction
strange that all these exemptions are of people who have to do with the enforcement of law? That is the point I would like cleared up. The Secretary of State says that the reason they have been exempted is that the judges' salaries .could not ibe reduced, without an amendment to the Judges Act. But why could not an amendment to the Judges Act be brought down simultaneously with this resolution? I do not see any difficulty in that regard. The sinister fact of the situation is that all those we are dealing with-judges, mounted police, military-have to do with the enforcement of law, and I .can come to no other conclusion than that they were exempted from the reduction in order that there might not be any dissatisfaction among those who had the enforcement of law in their hands. I protest against that with all the strength at my command.
There is another point I wish to make. Before these judges come those who are charged with contravening the law. You reduce the salary of a civil servant who is receiving less than $1,000. He has to keep himself and his family on that salary, and then because of economic pressure he is perhaps driven to do something in contravention of the law, and is brought before the judge, a judge drawing a comfortable salary. I would like to know how a judge in that position could pass sentence upon a person who is living in such different circumstances. There is no possible reason that I can find for these exemptions except that the government are fearful of what may happen in this country because ^ of the depressed condition of the people owing to the hardships which they have to put up with. The government do not want to be put in the position that Great Britain was in when she .made a reduction in the pay of the navy. The government is afraid of what may happen. I think they should at least have the courage to treat the whole civil service alike. If any further legislation is necessary it should be brought down at once. The government should show that it intends to legislate for the whole country on the basis of the democratic principles to which we have been accustomed in the past.

Before the Minister of Finance rises-I know he has had a very hard afternoon-I would plead with him to reconsider the position in which the prevailing rates men will be .put if a further reduction of ten per cent is made. It is quite evident from what was said in the house this afternoon by another minister of the crown that private employers having already reduced the wages of labourers, the government has reduced the
wages of its employees to the same level. What I want to point out to the minister, and I know he will get the point, is that in the event of the government reducing the prevailing rate men another ten per cent, private employers will insist on their men coming down to the same level as the government men, because they will say that the government rate is the prevailing rate.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
If my hon. friend is referring to this salary reduction as a cut in wages,
I do not follow him.

The Minister of Railways and Canals admitted to-day that he had already cut the wages of the men on a certain job because he found that the government had been paying more than the prevailing rate paid by the private employers in that district.
I shall not argue that point. But as a consequence the rates for the government prevailing rate men in that district are now on a level with the rate paid to labourers of private employers, and my point is that if the minister gives these prevailing rate men another ten per cent cut, private employers will bring down their wages to the same level by reducing them ten per cent.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I can only repeat to my hon. friend that I do not regard this resolution as effecting a salary reduction. Call it anything you like, but the salary remains the same. That is what I say.
They do not get the money, that is all.

I know that when I go
home after this session I shall figure that my indemnity has been reduced by ten per cent. I want to be helpful to the minister. I want him to get this point and I know that he will be fair enough to see that in those cases where men have already been cut-

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: If I understand my hon. friend aright, he is suggesting a sort of hide-and-go-seek game as 'between the government employees and private employees. I do not think he would seriously argue anything of the kind.

I hope Hansard gets me
correctly. I am afraid I am something like the Minister of Railways and Canals; I am thinking one thing and saying another. I want to impress upon the minister, however, that where the prevailing rate of wages has already been reduced, no further cuts should be made. Such action on the part of the government would be an inducement to private employers to cut still further the

wages of their men. If that were the case, the 'different governmental departments would have to make further wage cuts down to the prevailing rate among private employers, and there would be no end to it. I hope the minister will keep that in mind when he presents his bill.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I think the fears of the
hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River are quite unnecessary; he need have no misgiving whatsoever on that score.

It is quite clear that
at least on one point we have come to agreement, namely, with regard to the statutory obligations we owe to judges. That argument would seem to have fallen on the ground and must be abandoned. Speaking of the exemptions on February 26, the Prime Minister said that owing to the peculiar statutory position of judges, an exemption would be made in their case, and that among others to receive similar consideration would be railway commissioners. Turning to page 28 of the estimates I find that among the payments authorized by statute are the salaries of the Board of Railway Commissioners. It would seem to me therefore that there can be no legal argument upon the question of statutory obligation so far as judges are concerned, so that the discussion resolves itself into a consideration of the propriety of the action.
Following the argument of the Minister of Finance, and accepting his statement that no reduction in the salaries of judges is contemplated, I suggest that we should permit the judges among others, to accept this temporary sacrifice and equalize the burden on all sides.

I should like to ask the Minister of Finance a question. I have great difficulty in understanding how he reconciles, in regard to both grading and exemptions, the position he takes as Minister of Finance dealing with income tax legislation, and the position he takes as Minister of Finance dealing with this reduction in salary. How does my hon. friend, on the one hand dealing with the income tax, defend a graduated tax which bears less heavily upon those receiving small incomes and more heavily upon those whose incomes are large, while, as Minister of Finance dealing with civil service salaries he urges there should be a horizontal cut which leaves out altogether any graded arrangement?
_ Further, how does he, in dealing with the income tax, justify an exemption of small salaries on the score that the people receiving 
such salaries are least able to pay, but when dealing with a reduction of salaries of public servants exempt the largest salaries to the exclusion of all others? I remember that when the budget was introduced last year such exemptions as there were to a further upward gradation under the income tax were upon the large salaries. The present Minister of Finance was not in that office at that time; it would almost seem that the hand which had to do with the budget of last year had something to do with the drafting of these salary exemptions. I should like to know how my friend the present Minister of Finance justifies the exemption of high salaries, so far as these reductions in salaries of the public service are concerned, and goes to the opposite extreme when it comes to exemptions under income tax legislation, namely, exempting not the highest but the lowest salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Mr. Chairman, I assure my right hon. friend there is no deduction to be made to the effect that the person who drafted the income tax of last year is the one who drafted this resolution. I can assure my right hon. friend upon that point.
Or inspired it?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: As a matter of fact he had no knowledge of it. If there were no income tax I could see the force of my right hon. friend's argument when he says there should be a graduation with respect to the contribution being asked from civil servants this year. Inasmuch however as there are income taxes, if my right hon. friend would carry his argument reductio ad absurdum, he would finally leave the high salaried men with no salary whatever. In the circumstances I regard the cut of ten per cent as the one more equitable in the circumstances.

What about exemptions? My hon. friend has not told us how he justifies in the case of income tax exemptions of those who have small salaries and no exemptions of those who have high salaries, whereas, in the present instance he justifies the exemption of high salaries and does not permit an exemption in low salaries.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext:
I was not referring to
exemptions; probably there has been too much discussion on that score.

If my hon. friend will let us have an answer to my question, we may be able to get to the next stage on the resolution.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: I may have misapprehended my right hon. friend's meaning; I hope he is not objecting to the fact that we have made exemptions in the lower salaries.

I am trying to get at the principle which governs. My hon. friend will agree that in regard to income tax, exemptions are made on the salaries of those who have small incomes, but not on large incomes.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Or dependents.
On the principle of the tax bearing on those best able to carry it.

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: Yes.

That is the
principle there laid down and acted upon. If that principle is carried through in matters of taxation generally, how does he justify the exemption of the largest incomes, so far as these deductions in salaries are concerned?

speakerposition: Minister of Finance and Receiver General
speechtext: May I answer my right hon. friend in this way: In the first place he must remember that the higher salaries are subject to the dominion income tax, a graded tax bearing more heavily upon the higher salaries. The same principle applies to those who pay municipal income taxes. In some cases civil servants have to pay three income taxes- dominion, provincial and municipal. As I had pointed out to me, in one province the income tax has been doubled. That means that there is a very substantial portion of the salary of the highly paid officials taken away. If the reductions now before us were to be continued and were based upon an expectation of permanency, my right hon. friend's question might be an appropriate one for discussion at this point, and we might consider whether the system of grading should apply. In this instance however there is only one contribution for one year, and I submit that the method suggested by the government is the fair one.

I wish to make it clear that I am not objecting to the cut in indemnities, but I am objecting to the cut as it applies to civil servants.
